content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › RIPv2 Implementation

RIPv2 Implementation and Verification

From enabling the process to securing updates, this chapter covers the commands and checks you need for a reliable RIPv2 lab or production testbed.

In this lesson

Enable RIPv2, set version 2, add network statements correctly, and disable auto-summary when using VLSM.

Coming up

Use passive-interface for access LANs, configure MD5 authentication with key chains, and verify with show and debug commands.

Concept Map
Configuration → Timers → Verification → Authentication
Example
A two-router lab advertises loopbacks and a LAN. R1 and R2 exchange routes on Gi0/0 with MD5. Gi0/1 on R2 is passive so updates are not sent to end hosts.
Why it matters
RIPv2 is simple and useful for labs and small networks but requires careful configuration to avoid incorrect advertisements or lost routes due to mismatched authentication or auto-summary behavior.
Explore Key Topics
Config Essentials
router rip, version 2, network <classful>, no auto-summary.
Timers
Update, invalid, holddown, flush control convergence and route lifecycle.
Security
Use key chains and MD5 authentication. Both sides must match or adjacency fails.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your hands-on work and checks. First, you'll configure RIPv2 correctly on Cisco IOS by enabling the router process, forcing version 2, and using classful network statements so interfaces are properly included. Second, you'll learn to apply passive-interface to ports serving only hosts so updates are not sent where they're unnecessary. Third, you'll understand RIP timers — update, invalid, holddown, and flush — and how they affect how quickly routes appear or disappear. Fourth, you'll verify RIPv2 with show and debug commands to confirm routes and adjacency details. Each objective links a command set to a measurable verification step so you can confirm competency in a lab or troubleshooting scenario. As you practice, keep in mind a short checklist: ensure version 2 is set, check network statements align to classful networks, disable auto-summary when using VLSM, and confirm authentication keys match. This guided focus will get you from configuration to confident verification.

Configure RIPv2

Enable the RIP process, set version 2, and use classful network statements to ensure interfaces participate. This prevents accidental omission of interfaces and supports VLSM when combined with no auto-summary.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Use passive-interface

Stop RIP updates from leaving interfaces that connect only to end hosts while still advertising their networks. This reduces unnecessary traffic and limits exposure of routing updates.

screens.title: Enabling RIPv2 and classful network statements
screens.narratorSegment: To enable RIPv2 you start the RIP routing process and explicitly choose version 2. The core commands are router rip and version 2. After that you use network statements to tell the router which directly connected networks to advertise. A key detail is that RIP's network command matches classful network addresses, not specific subnets or host addresses. For example, an interface with address 192.168.1.1/24 is included by network 192.168.1.0 because RIP considers the classful network. A common mistake is entering the host IP or subnet like 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.1.0/24 in some form; in RIP you should specify the classful base. If you omit version 2, older IOS releases may default to RIPv1 which does not support CIDR and VLSM, causing incorrect route advertisement. Practically, after you configure router rip, version 2, and your network lines, check show ip protocols to confirm the RIP process is active and which interfaces are participating. Try a quick mental test: if an interface is 10.1.1.1/24, which network statement will include it? The answer is the classful network 10.0.0.0. This classful behavior defines how RIP discovers which interfaces join the process and advertise routes.

keyIdea.title: Enable RIPv2 precisely
keyIdea.text: Use router rip, set version 2, and supply classful network addresses so the router enables RIP on the correct interfaces.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Enable RIPv2
Definition

router rip and network statements

Starting the RIP process registers the routing protocol. The network commands indicate which classful networks' interfaces should run RIP and be advertised to neighbors.

Concrete example
router rip
 version 2
 network 192.168.1.0
 network 10.0.0.0
Note: network 192.168.1.0 is the classful network used to match an interface address like 192.168.1.1/24.
Common mistake

Using a host or subnet in the network command or forgetting version 2. For instance, network 192.168.1.1 is incorrect for RIP; use the classful base address instead.

Tip
Always run show ip protocols after configuring to confirm version and participating interfaces.
Key Takeaway

RIP's network command maps to classful networks. Set version 2 to support VLSM and avoid RIPv1 behavior.

screens.title: Disabling auto-summarization and handling VLSM
screens.narratorSegment: RIPv2 supports classless routing, but it historically performs auto-summarization at classful boundaries unless you turn it off. The no auto-summary command under router rip prevents RIP from summarizing subnets to their natural classful network when advertisements cross major network boundaries. In practical terms, when you use variable-length subnet masks or have discontiguous networks that share classful prefixes, auto-summarization can cause incorrect route masks to be advertised and learned by other routers. This leads to traffic black-holing or suboptimal routing. The typical sequence is to configure router rip, version 2, add network statements, and then issue no auto-summary to ensure routes are advertised with their actual subnet masks. You should verify behavior with show ip route rip to confirm that learned entries include the correct mask. A common misconception is that RIPv2 always preserves subnet masks — that is only true when auto-summary is disabled or when advertisements do not cross classful boundaries. Use no auto-summary in most modern networks that use VLSM. Think of no auto-summary as preserving the precise address information so routing decisions remain correct across the domain.

keyIdea.title: Preserve subnet detail
keyIdea.text: Use no auto-summary so RIPv2 advertises routes with their actual subnet masks, avoiding incorrect summarization across boundaries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › no auto-summary
Process

Disable auto-summarization

Auto-summary can convert specific subnets back to their classful parent when routes traverse classful boundaries. With VLSM and discontiguous networks this loses critical mask info. Use no auto-summary to prevent that.

Step 1
Under router rip run no auto-summary.
Step 2
Check show ip route rip to see masks retained.
Step 3
If problems appear, verify network statements and interface IP masks.
Example
Under router rip, include no auto-summary to keep route masks when advertising 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24 that share a 10.0.0.0 classful network.
Misconception
Don't assume RIPv2 will always keep subnet masks. If auto-summary is on and routes cross classful boundaries, masks may be lost.
Key Takeaway

Disable auto-summarization in modern VLSM networks to retain precise route masks across the RIP domain.

screens.title: Passive interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Passive-interface is a targeted way to stop RIP updates from traversing an interface while still advertising the connected network to other RIP neighbors. You typically use passive-interface on segments that contain only end hosts and no RIP neighbors, such as a LAN that connects PCs or servers. The command is configured under the router rip process as passive-interface followed by the interface name. When you apply it, the router keeps the network in its advertisements to other neighbors but stops sending periodic RIP updates out that interface. This reduces unnecessary churn and reduces the exposure of routing information to devices that do not need it. A concrete example is a router R2 with Gi0/1 connected to a LAN; configure passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on R2 so the LAN is advertised to other routers but R2 does not send RIP packets into the LAN. A common mistake is to apply passive-interface globally without verifying that a neighbor exists on that interface; applying it on an interface with a router neighbor will prevent adjacency creation. Always verify the passive state with show ip protocols and confirm routes with show ip route rip after configuring.

keyIdea.title: Control update propagation
keyIdea.text: Use passive-interface to advertise a network but prevent RIP updates from being sent on interfaces that face hosts only.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Passive Interface
What it does

Advertise but don't send

Passive-interface tells RIP not to transmit updates on a specific interface while still advertising that network to other neighbors on active interfaces.

Command example
router rip
 version 2
 network 192.168.2.0
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 no auto-summary
Concrete scenario
On R2, Gi0/1 connects to a LAN with only hosts. Configure passive-interface Gi0/1 so host devices do not receive RIP updates, but other routers still learn the LAN network.
Common mistake

Don't make an interface passive if a neighboring router lives there; that will prevent RIP adjacency from forming and break route exchange.

Key Takeaway

Use passive-interface to reduce unnecessary RIP traffic and secure LANs that do not need routing updates.

screens.title: RIP Timers explained
screens.narratorSegment: RIP relies on a set of timers to control how often updates are sent and how the router treats potentially stale routes. The update timer, default 30 seconds, is the interval at which routers broadcast their routing information. The invalid timer, default 180 seconds, defines how long a route may go without being refreshed before it is marked invalid. When a route is marked invalid it may trigger holddown behavior; the holddown timer, default 180 seconds, is the period during which the router will not accept newer routing information for that route that might be unstable, helping prevent routing loops. The flush timer, default 240 seconds, determines how long an invalid route remains in the routing table before it is removed entirely. You can adjust these with the timers basic command under router rip, but changing them affects convergence: shorter timers increase churn and C P U usage; longer timers slow recovery. A concrete example: if a neighbor stops sending updates, the route will be marked invalid after the invalid timer expires and will be flushed later. A misconception is assuming holddown always makes convergence faster — in truth it prevents premature acceptance of possibly incorrect updates but can slow adoption of legitimate alternate paths. Always balance timer changes against network size and stability.

keyIdea.text: RIP timers regulate update frequency and route lifecycle; adjust them cautiously because they trade convergence speed against stability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › RIP Timers
Timer reference

Update / Invalid / Holddown / Flush

Update Timer
Default 30s. How often full routing updates are sent to neighbors.
Invalid Timer
Default 180s. Time without updates before a route is marked invalid.
Holddown Timer
Default 180s. Prevents accepting potentially unstable updates while network stabilizes.
Flush Timer
Default 240s. When a route is removed from the routing table after being invalid.
Adjustment
Use timers basic under router rip to change values. Changing timers affects convergence and stability; adjust only when needed.
Misconception
Shorter timers always help convergence — not always. They can cause extra CPU and route flapping in unstable networks.
Key Takeaway

Know default timers, verify behavior with show ip protocols, and change timers only with a clear reason and testing plan.

screens.title: Using show and debug to verify RIPv2
screens.narratorSegment: Verification gives you confidence that your configuration is working. show ip protocols summarizes the routing processes on a router and shows RIP version, timers, and which interfaces are participating. Use show ip route rip to display only the routes learned via RIP and examine their metrics. show ip rip database can give more granular RIP-specific information if you need to inspect internal RIP structures. debug ip rip prints live RIP update packets being sent and received, which is invaluable during lab troubleshooting but should be used carefully in production because debug output can consume C P U and flood terminals. Typical workflow: after configuration run show ip protocols to confirm version 2 and passive interfaces, then run show ip route rip to confirm learned routes from neighbors. If routes are missing, ping across the link to ensure basic IP connectivity, then use debug ip rip during a controlled test to capture live exchange. A key distinction: show commands are non-intrusive and should be your first step; debug is intrusive and used after you verify connectivity. End with this check: if show ip protocols lists the interface but show ip route rip is empty, authentication mismatch or incorrect network statements are likely causes.

keyIdea.text: Start with non-intrusive show commands; use debug ip rip only in controlled troubleshooting to inspect live update packets.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Verify RIPv2
Show commands

Quick checks

show ip protocols
Shows RIP version, timers, and participating interfaces including passive-interface listings.
show ip route rip
Lists routes learned via RIP and their hop-count metrics.
show ip rip database
Provides RIP-specific database details when needed.
Debugging

debug ip rip

Use debug to view live update exchanges. Only enable in controlled labs or during maintenance windows and be prepared to turn it off quickly.

Example workflow
  1. Run show ip protocols and show ip route rip.
  2. If routes missing, ping neighbor to confirm IP connectivity.
  3. If connectivity OK, enable debug ip rip for targeted capture.
Key Takeaway

Start with show commands, validate connectivity, then use debug ip rip as a last, controlled step to inspect updates.

screens.title: RIPv2 MD5 authentication with key chains
screens.narratorSegment: Securing RIP updates prevents unauthorized injection of routes. RIPv2 supports message digest 5 authentication using a key chain. The process is: create a key chain with key and key-string, then apply that key chain to the interface where RIP updates are exchanged with ip rip authentication key-chain and set ip rip authentication mode md5. Both ends of the link must use the same key chain and authentication mode for adjacency to form. For example, define key chain RIP_AUTH with key 1 and key-string CohortiaRocks!, then on the interface apply ip rip authentication key-chain RIP_AUTH and ip rip authentication mode md5. If authentication fails because the key strings differ or mode mismatches, neighbors will not exchange routes and routes learned via RIP will disappear. When troubleshooting, confirm key chain definitions, check interface authentication commands, and verify with show ip protocols that interfaces are participating correctly. A practical diagnostic is intentionally misconfiguring the key on one side to observe route disappearance, then fixing the key to confirm restoration. Remember that authentication secures updates but also creates a single point of adjacency failure if misconfigured.

keyIdea.title: Authentication prevents route injection
keyIdea.text: Use key chains and MD5 authentication and ensure both sides match to keep RIP adjacencies healthy and secure.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › MD5 Authentication
Definition

Key chains and md5

Define a key chain and apply it to the interface to require MD5-authenticated RIP updates from the neighbor.

Configuration example
! On Router A and Router B
key chain RIP_AUTH
 key 1
  key-string CohortiaRocks!
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip rip authentication key-chain RIP_AUTH
 ip rip authentication mode md5
Troubleshoot
If neighbors fail to exchange routes, compare key chain names, key numbers, and key-strings on both sides and verify the interface authentication mode is md5.
Observation

Mismatched keys cause route disappearance — fix keys to restore adjacency and routes.

Key Takeaway

Authentication secures updates but requires exact configuration on both peers; use it for any link where security matters.

screens.title: Hands-on: Configure the R1–R2 topology
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the provided two-router topology. Start by assigning IPs on each router's interfaces and loopbacks. On R1, enable RIPv2 with router rip and version 2, advertise the classful networks that include the interfaces and loopback, and disable auto-summary so subnets are preserved. On R2 do the same and add passive-interface to the LAN-facing port so RIP updates aren't sent to hosts. After initial configuration verify with show ip protocols and show ip route rip to ensure each router learns the other's loopback networks. Next configure MD5 authentication using a key chain named RIP_AUTH with key 1 and a key-string that matches on both routers, then apply ip rip authentication key-chain RIP_AUTH and ip rip authentication mode md5 to the link interfaces. If routes disappear after authentication, check the key-string typos first. During the lab use ping to verify IP connectivity before running debug ip rip. This controlled sequence — configure, verify connectivity, enable authentication, verify routes — is the safest path to a working and secure RIP adjacency. Hands-on: Configure the R1–R2 topology means configure addresses, enable ripv2 with version 2 and no auto-summary, set passive-interface for host lans, then add md5 authentication and verify with show commands.. In practical terms, step-by-step ripv2 configuration, passive interface, and timers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common RIPv2 mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When RIP behavior doesn't match expectations, a short checklist will often find the problem. First, confirm IP connectivity with ping and traceroute. If pings fail, fix addressing or layer-2 issues before checking RIP. If connectivity is fine but routes are missing, verify you set version 2 and used classful network statements — entering a host address in the network command is a common cause of missing interfaces. If learned routes show but masks are wrong, ensure no auto-summary is configured. For authentication failures check that key chain names, key numbers, key-strings, and ip rip authentication mode match on both routers. Use show ip protocols to see which interfaces are active or passive. If debug ip rip is required, enable it in a lab or maintenance window and watch for rejected updates or authentication errors in the debug output. A typical troubleshooting sequence is: ping neighbor, show ip protocols, show ip route rip, confirm key chains, then debug if necessary. Keep in mind that holddown and timer settings can delay route acceptance or removal — adjust timers only with reasoned testing. This checklist helps you rapidly narrow a problem to connectivity, configuration, authentication, or timer behavior.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
Checklist

Step-by-step

  1. Ping the neighbor IP to verify L3 reachability.
  2. Run show ip protocols to confirm version and passive-interface state.
  3. Run show ip route rip to inspect learned routes and masks.
  4. Check key chains and interface authentication if adjacency missing.
  5. Use debug ip rip in a lab if further packet-level detail is required.
Common failures
Wrong network statement
Using a host or subnet instead of classful base leads to missing interfaces in RIP.
Authentication mismatch
Mismatched key-strings or modes prevent adjacency and make routes disappear.
Timers
Holddown and invalid timers influence when routes are marked invalid or flushed; understand defaults before changing them.
Key Takeaway

Work from connectivity to configuration to authentication; each step narrows the fault domain efficiently.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to turn the RIP routing process into a functioning, secure set of routes on Cisco routers. We'll focus on enabling RIPv2 correctly, advertising the right networks using classful network statements, and avoiding a common mistake of supplying a host or subnet instead of the classful network. You will also learn how to disable auto-summarization to preserve subnet masks across VLSM and discontiguous networks. We'll show how to use passive-interface to stop unnecessary updates on access LANs, and we'll explore RIP timers — update, invalid, holddown, and flush — so you understand convergence behavior. Verification is practical: you'll use show ip protocols, show ip route rip, and debug ip rip carefully. Finally, we'll demonstrate MD5 authentication with key chains and how mismatched keys cause routes to disappear. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to configure a two-router lab, secure the RIP adjacency, verify routes, and diagnose common mistakes. Think about a simple question as you go: is the network statement matching the classful network of my interface?

These objectives focus your hands-on work and checks. First, you'll configure RIPv2 correctly on Cisco IOS by enabling the router process, forcing version 2, and using classful network statements so interfaces are properly included. Second, you'll learn to apply passive-interface to ports serving only hosts so updates are not sent where they're unnecessary. Third, you'll understand RIP timers — update, invalid, holddown, and flush — and how they affect how quickly routes appear or disappear. Fourth, you'll verify RIPv2 with show and debug commands to confirm routes and adjacency details. Each objective links a command set to a measurable verification step so you can confirm competency in a lab or troubleshooting scenario. As you practice, keep in mind a short checklist: ensure version 2 is set, check network statements align to classful networks, disable auto-summary when using VLSM, and confirm authentication keys match. This guided focus will get you from configuration to confident verification.

Continuing the objectives, you'll implement MD5 authentication using key chains and apply authentication to interfaces exchanging RIP. This makes sure that only routers with matching keys exchange routes; if keys differ, adjacencies fail and routes disappear. You'll also identify common configuration mistakes such as using host or subnet addresses instead of the classful network in network statements, forgetting to set version 2, or leaving auto-summary enabled in VLSM environments. Finally, you'll practice a small lab that walks through configuring R1 and R2, adding loopback networks, making one interface passive, and verifying routes with show ip route rip. Each objective ties a configuration step to a verification step so you can quickly diagnose whether a mistake is configuration, authentication, or connectivity. When troubleshooting, always confirm basic IP connectivity with ping before deeper RIP debug steps.

To enable RIPv2 you start the RIP routing process and explicitly choose version 2. The core commands are router rip and version 2. After that you use network statements to tell the router which directly connected networks to advertise. A key detail is that RIP's network command matches classful network addresses, not specific subnets or host addresses. For example, an interface with address 192.168.1.1/24 is included by network 192.168.1.0 because RIP considers the classful network. A common mistake is entering the host IP or subnet like 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.1.0/24 in some form; in RIP you should specify the classful base. If you omit version 2, older IOS releases may default to RIPv1 which does not support CIDR and VLSM, causing incorrect route advertisement. Practically, after you configure router rip, version 2, and your network lines, check show ip protocols to confirm the RIP process is active and which interfaces are participating. Try a quick mental test: if an interface is 10.1.1.1/24, which network statement will include it? The answer is the classful network 10.0.0.0. This classful behavior defines how RIP discovers which interfaces join the process and advertise routes.

RIPv2 supports classless routing, but it historically performs auto-summarization at classful boundaries unless you turn it off. The no auto-summary command under router rip prevents RIP from summarizing subnets to their natural classful network when advertisements cross major network boundaries. In practical terms, when you use variable-length subnet masks or have discontiguous networks that share classful prefixes, auto-summarization can cause incorrect route masks to be advertised and learned by other routers. This leads to traffic black-holing or suboptimal routing. The typical sequence is to configure router rip, version 2, add network statements, and then issue no auto-summary to ensure routes are advertised with their actual subnet masks. You should verify behavior with show ip route rip to confirm that learned entries include the correct mask. A common misconception is that RIPv2 always preserves subnet masks — that is only true when auto-summary is disabled or when advertisements do not cross classful boundaries. Use no auto-summary in most modern networks that use VLSM. Think of no auto-summary as preserving the precise address information so routing decisions remain correct across the domain.

Passive-interface is a targeted way to stop RIP updates from traversing an interface while still advertising the connected network to other RIP neighbors. You typically use passive-interface on segments that contain only end hosts and no RIP neighbors, such as a LAN that connects PCs or servers. The command is configured under the router rip process as passive-interface followed by the interface name. When you apply it, the router keeps the network in its advertisements to other neighbors but stops sending periodic RIP updates out that interface. This reduces unnecessary churn and reduces the exposure of routing information to devices that do not need it. A concrete example is a router R2 with Gi0/1 connected to a LAN; configure passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on R2 so the LAN is advertised to other routers but R2 does not send RIP packets into the LAN. A common mistake is to apply passive-interface globally without verifying that a neighbor exists on that interface; applying it on an interface with a router neighbor will prevent adjacency creation. Always verify the passive state with show ip protocols and confirm routes with show ip route rip after configuring.

RIP relies on a set of timers to control how often updates are sent and how the router treats potentially stale routes. The update timer, default 30 seconds, is the interval at which routers broadcast their routing information. The invalid timer, default 180 seconds, defines how long a route may go without being refreshed before it is marked invalid. When a route is marked invalid it may trigger holddown behavior; the holddown timer, default 180 seconds, is the period during which the router will not accept newer routing information for that route that might be unstable, helping prevent routing loops. The flush timer, default 240 seconds, determines how long an invalid route remains in the routing table before it is removed entirely. You can adjust these with the timers basic command under router rip, but changing them affects convergence: shorter timers increase churn and C P U usage; longer timers slow recovery. A concrete example: if a neighbor stops sending updates, the route will be marked invalid after the invalid timer expires and will be flushed later. A misconception is assuming holddown always makes convergence faster — in truth it prevents premature acceptance of possibly incorrect updates but can slow adoption of legitimate alternate paths. Always balance timer changes against network size and stability.

Verification gives you confidence that your configuration is working. show ip protocols summarizes the routing processes on a router and shows RIP version, timers, and which interfaces are participating. Use show ip route rip to display only the routes learned via RIP and examine their metrics. show ip rip database can give more granular RIP-specific information if you need to inspect internal RIP structures. debug ip rip prints live RIP update packets being sent and received, which is invaluable during lab troubleshooting but should be used carefully in production because debug output can consume C P U and flood terminals. Typical workflow: after configuration run show ip protocols to confirm version 2 and passive interfaces, then run show ip route rip to confirm learned routes from neighbors. If routes are missing, ping across the link to ensure basic IP connectivity, then use debug ip rip during a controlled test to capture live exchange. A key distinction: show commands are non-intrusive and should be your first step; debug is intrusive and used after you verify connectivity. End with this check: if show ip protocols lists the interface but show ip route rip is empty, authentication mismatch or incorrect network statements are likely causes.

Securing RIP updates prevents unauthorized injection of routes. RIPv2 supports message digest 5 authentication using a key chain. The process is: create a key chain with key and key-string, then apply that key chain to the interface where RIP updates are exchanged with ip rip authentication key-chain and set ip rip authentication mode md5. Both ends of the link must use the same key chain and authentication mode for adjacency to form. For example, define key chain RIP_AUTH with key 1 and key-string CohortiaRocks!, then on the interface apply ip rip authentication key-chain RIP_AUTH and ip rip authentication mode md5. If authentication fails because the key strings differ or mode mismatches, neighbors will not exchange routes and routes learned via RIP will disappear. When troubleshooting, confirm key chain definitions, check interface authentication commands, and verify with show ip protocols that interfaces are participating correctly. A practical diagnostic is intentionally misconfiguring the key on one side to observe route disappearance, then fixing the key to confirm restoration. Remember that authentication secures updates but also creates a single point of adjacency failure if misconfigured.

This walkthrough follows the provided two-router topology. Start by assigning IPs on each router's interfaces and loopbacks. On R1, enable RIPv2 with router rip and version 2, advertise the classful networks that include the interfaces and loopback, and disable auto-summary so subnets are preserved. On R2 do the same and add passive-interface to the LAN-facing port so RIP updates aren't sent to hosts. After initial configuration verify with show ip protocols and show ip route rip to ensure each router learns the other's loopback networks. Next configure MD5 authentication using a key chain named RIP_AUTH with key 1 and a key-string that matches on both routers, then apply ip rip authentication key-chain RIP_AUTH and ip rip authentication mode md5 to the link interfaces. If routes disappear after authentication, check the key-string typos first. During the lab use ping to verify IP connectivity before running debug ip rip. This controlled sequence — configure, verify connectivity, enable authentication, verify routes — is the safest path to a working and secure RIP adjacency.
